customLessons.title: Physical Properties of Materials
objectives: Describe and classify materials based on observable physical properties: color, texture, hardness, flexibility, transparency, absorbency, magnetism, and ability to float or sink.
Connect physical properties of materials with everyday applications (e.g., cloth for absorbency, clear glass for transparency, metals for durable tools).
Perform guided classroom investigations applying physical properties to select materials for specific real-life purposes.
customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 1: Physical Properties of Materials
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Classify materials based on observable physical properties and select materials for specific real-life purposes.

WHAT ARE PHYSICAL PROPERTIES?
Physical properties are characteristics of a material that can be observed or measured without changing the material into something else.

KEY OBSERVABLE PROPERTIES:
• Color and Texture: Smooth glass, rough sandpaper, soft cotton.
• Hardness: A material's resistance to scratching or indentation (bending is related to flexibility). Example: Hard metals resist scratching and are used for tools.
• Flexibility: Ability to bend without breaking. Example: Rubber bands and plastic rulers.
• Transparency: Allowing light to pass through. Example: Clear glass window panes allow us to see outside.
• Absorbency: Ability to take in liquid into internal pores. Example: Cotton cloth absorbs water quickly for bath towels.
• Magnetism: Being attracted to a magnet. Example: Iron nails and steel paperclips are magnetic.
• Ability to Float or Sink: Depends on density and buoyancy. Objects less dense than water float (wood, oil), while denser objects sink (iron nails, stones).

APPLICATIONS IN DAILY LIFE:
• Cloth → High absorbency for bath towels and kitchen wiping cloths.
• Clear Glass → High transparency for classroom windows and spectacles.
• Metals → High hardness and strength for construction hammers and security gates.

INTERACTIVE ACTIVITY: Choose the Right Material!
Situation: You need to clean spilled juice on your study table. Which material should you pick?
A) Plastic sheet  B) Cotton cloth  C) Glass pane
Answer: B — Cotton cloth, because of its high absorbency!

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Observable physical properties help us identify and classify materials.
• Hardness is resistance to scratching and denting.
• Floating and sinking depend on density and buoyant force in water.
• We select materials based on matching their properties to their everyday functions.

slides.title: Physical Properties of Materials
slides.content:
Grade 4 — Quarter 1: Matter and Materials
(Validated Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

Discover how color, texture, hardness, flexibility, transparency, absorbency, and buoyancy help us select materials for daily life.

slides.title: Observable Physical Properties
slides.content:
Characteristics observed without altering chemical identity:
• Hardness: Resistance to scratching/indentation (bending is flexibility!)
• Flexibility: Ability to bend without snapping
• Transparency: Letting light pass through clearly (glass windows)
• Absorbency: Drawing liquids into pores (cotton bath towels)
• Magnetism: Attracted to magnetic poles (iron, steel)

slides.title: Density & Buoyancy: Floating vs Sinking
slides.content:
Why do some objects float while others sink?
• Floating or sinking depends on density (mass per volume) and buoyant force!
• Objects with lower density than water float (wood, hollow plastic bottles)
• Objects denser than water sink (solid iron nails, pebbles)
• Steel ships float because their hollow hull encloses air, lowering average density.
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Fill clear basin with water
Step 2: Gently place wood block -> Floats (low density)
Step 3: Drop solid iron nail -> Sinks (high density)
Step 4: Shape clay into a boat -> Floats due to buoyancy!

slides.title: Matching Properties to Practical Uses
slides.content:
Why we choose specific materials:
• Bath Towels: Cotton cloth for high absorbency
• Window Panes: Clear glass for high optical transparency
• Construction Tools: Iron and steel for high hardness and strength
• Electrical Grips: Rubber for flexible insulation

slides.title: Assessment: Physical Properties
slides.content:
Check Your Understanding (Validated Answer Key: 1-B, 2-A, 3-C, 4-C, 5-A):
1. Hardness measures resistance to scratching/indentation (B)
2. Bath towels require high absorbency (A)
3. Floating occurs when buoyant force balances weight due to lower density (C)
4. Window panes require optical transparency (C)
5. Construction hammers require high hardness and durability (A)

customLessons.title: Chemical Properties of Materials
objectives: Identify and describe chemical properties of everyday materials: burning, rusting, reacting, decay, degradation, and biodegradation.
Differentiate natural decay and biodegradation from non-biodegradable synthetic persistence.
Practice classroom safety guidelines regarding reactive and flammable materials under teacher guidance.
customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 2: Chemical Properties of Materials
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Identify and describe chemical properties of everyday materials.

WHAT IS A CHEMICAL PROPERTY?
A chemical property describes how a material behaves when it interacts with another substance or undergoes a chemical change, transforming into a new substance.

KEY CHEMICAL PROPERTIES:
• Burning (Flammability): How easily a material catches fire in the presence of oxygen. Paper and dry wood burn, producing smoke and ash.
• Rusting (Corrosion): Iron and steel react slowly with oxygen and moisture from the air to form reddish-brown rust (iron oxide).
• Reacting with Other Substances: Baking soda reacts vigorously with vinegar, releasing bubbling carbon dioxide gas.
• Decay and Degradation: Breakdown of materials over time through exposure to weather and chemical action.
• Biodegradation: The breakdown of organic matter (fruit peels, leaves, food scraps) through the natural action of living microorganisms like bacteria and fungi, returning nutrients to the soil.

CLASSROOM SAFETY NOTICE:
Learners must NEVER conduct open burning experiments! All demonstrations involving fire, hot surfaces, or reactive chemicals must be strictly teacher-guided using safe multimedia visuals and videos.

INTERACTIVE ACTIVITY: Identify the Chemical Property!
1. An iron gate turns reddish-brown after rainy weeks. → Rusting (reaction with moisture & oxygen)
2. Fallen mango leaves rot and disappear into garden soil. → Biodegradation / Decay
3. Dry paper ignites when exposed to a flame. → Burning / Flammability

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Chemical properties involve how materials react to form new substances.
• Rusting requires both moisture and oxygen.
• Biodegradation is a biological breakdown process by microorganisms.
• Always follow classroom safety rules around reactive materials.

slides.title: Chemical Properties of Materials
slides.content:
Grade 4 — Quarter 1: Matter and Materials
(Validated Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

Investigate how materials react, burn, rust, and biodegrade into new substances.

slides.title: Chemical Property vs Chemical Change
slides.content:
Defining the reaction potential:
• Chemical Property: Describes a material's potential behavior when interacting with other substances (e.g., flammability, rust potential)
• Chemical Change: The actual process of changing into one or more new substances with different chemical properties!

slides.title: Rusting & Reactivity in Daily Life
slides.content:
Common Chemical Reactions:
• Rusting: Iron and steel react with oxygen and moisture in humid Philippine air
• Reacting: Vinegar + baking soda creates bubbling carbon dioxide gas
• Painting fences prevents rust by blocking oxygen and rainwater!
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Bare iron nail exposed to air
Step 2: Rainwater and oxygen touch iron surface
Step 3: Chemical reaction produces reddish iron oxide (rust)
Step 4: Protective paint stops the reaction

slides.title: Decay vs Biodegradation & Safety
slides.content:
Understanding decomposition:
• Biodegradation: Broader scientific term for breakdown of organic matter through microorganisms (leaves, fruit peels)
• Safety First: Learners must never burn materials! Visuals and teacher demonstrations ensure 100% classroom safety.

slides.title: Assessment: Chemical Properties
slides.content:
Check Your Understanding (Validated Answer Key: 1-C, 2-A, 3-B, 4-A, 5-C):
1. Iron and steel have the ability to rust when exposed to oxygen and moisture (C)
2. Biodegradation is the biological breakdown of organic matter (A)
3. Pupils avoid burning activities because open flames pose fire and smoke hazards (B)
4. A chemical property describes behavior when interacting with another substance (A)
5. Food scraps decay through biodegradation to enrich garden soil (C)

customLessons.title: Effects of Heat, Cooling, Air, and Water on Materials
objectives: Observe and describe physical and chemical changes caused by heat, cooling, air, and water.
Explain phase changes: melting, freezing (water to ice), evaporation, and drying.
Identify observable transformations including rust formation, decay of organic matter, and burning.
customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 3: Effects of Heat, Cooling, Air, and Water on Materials
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Describe observable changes in materials caused by heat, cooling, air, and water.

ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS CAUSING CHANGES:
1. Heat (Heating):
• Melting: Solid turns to liquid when heated (butter melting in a warm pan, candle wax softening).
• Evaporation / Drying: Heat causes liquid water to change into invisible water vapor and leave the material. Hanging wet laundry in the sun dries because water evaporates into the air!

2. Cooling (Freezing):
• Freezing: When liquid water is cooled to 0°C, it turns into solid ice. (Scientific note: For water turning to ice, the precise term is FREEZING, while 'hardening' applies to melted solids solidifying).

3. Air and Moisture (Water):
• Rusting: Moisture and oxygen in air cause iron nails and tin sheets to corrode into reddish-brown rust.
• Decaying / Spoiling: Food and bread left exposed to humid air develop mold and decay due to moisture and microscopic spores.

4. Burning (Teacher Demonstration Only):
• High heat in the presence of air burns dry wood and paper into ash and carbon dioxide gas.

INTERACTIVE ACTIVITY: Before and After!
• Water placed in a freezer → Liquid becomes solid ice (Freezing)
• Wet shirt hung under the sun → Water changes to vapor and leaves shirt (Evaporation/Drying)
• Solid candle wax warmed gently → Solid becomes liquid (Melting)
• Iron nail soaked in moist air → Gray metal forms reddish-brown coating (Rusting)

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Heating causes melting and evaporation (drying).
• Cooling liquid water causes freezing into ice.
• Air and water together cause iron rusting and organic decay.
• Scientists observe before-and-after conditions to track material changes.

slides.title: Effects of Heat, Cooling, Air, and Water
slides.content:
Grade 4 — Quarter 1: Matter and Materials
(Validated Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

Track how temperature and environmental factors transform everyday substances.

slides.title: Heat: Melting & Evaporative Drying
slides.content:
Observable Effects of Adding Heat:
• Melting: Solid butter or ice turns to liquid when heated
• Evaporation & Drying: Heat gives water molecules energy to turn into water vapor and escape into the air
• That is how wet clothes dry on the clothesline!

slides.title: Cooling: Freezing Water into Ice
slides.content:
Observable Effects of Removing Heat:
• Freezing: Liquid water cooled in a freezer turns into solid ice
• Precise scientific term: FREEZING (not hardening)
• Freezing is a reversible physical phase change!
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Pour liquid water into ice tray
Step 2: Place in freezer below 0°C
Step 3: Thermal energy leaves the water
Step 4: Molecules lock into solid ice crystals (Freezing)

slides.title: Air & Water: Rusting and Decay
slides.content:
Environmental Conditions at Work:
• Rusting: Iron nails left outdoors react with atmospheric oxygen and water droplets
• Decay: Bread and fruits exposed to moist warm air provide ideal conditions for fungal mold growth
• Both represent changes fueled by air and moisture!

slides.title: Assessment: Temperature & Environment
slides.content:
Check Your Understanding (Validated Answer Key: 1-B, 2-A, 3-B, 4-A, 5-A):
1. Liquid water cooling into solid ice is FREEZING (B)
2. Wet laundry dries because water evaporates into water vapor and leaves (A)
3. Solid butter heating in a pan undergoes MELTING (B)
4. Iron nails turn reddish-brown due to exposure to moisture and air (A)
5. Bread spoils in warm moisture because it decays and grows mold (A)

customLessons.title: Physical and Chemical Changes
objectives: Distinguish physical changes from chemical changes using observable evidence.
Explain that in physical changes, size, shape, or state may change, but no new material is formed.
Identify chemical changes characterized by the formation of new materials (burning, rusting, decay).
customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 4: Physical and Chemical Changes
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
Use observable evidence to distinguish physical changes from chemical changes.

THE CENTRAL DISTINCTION:
• Physical Change: The size, shape, or state/form of the material may change, but NO NEW MATERIAL IS FORMED.
  - Cutting paper: Small pieces of paper are still paper.
  - Folding clothes: Folded fabric is still fabric.
  - Crushing an aluminum can: Crushed metal is still aluminum.
  - Melting ice: Liquid water is chemically identical to solid ice.

• Chemical Change: A NEW MATERIAL IS FORMED with properties different from the original substances.
  - Burning wood: Cellulose breaks down into gray ash, carbon dioxide, and smoke.
  - Rusting iron: Iron and oxygen create a completely new substance: iron oxide (rust).
  - Decaying fruit: Rotten fruit produces new foul-smelling compounds and soft organic matter.

COMPARISON TABLE:
Feature | Physical Change | Chemical Change
New substance formed? | NO | YES
Reversible? | Often reversible | Difficult or impossible to reverse
Examples | Cutting, folding, melting, freezing | Burning, rusting, decaying, cooking

INTERACTIVE ACTIVITY: Physical or Chemical?
1. Slicing an apple into four wedges → Physical Change (still apple)
2. Leaving the apple slice out until it turns brown and rots → Chemical Change (decay/new substance)
3. Crushing a dry chalk stick into fine powder → Physical Change (still chalk)
4. Striking a matchstick to produce flame and smoke → Chemical Change (combustion)

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Physical changes alter size, shape, or state without forming new materials.
• Chemical changes produce new substances with observable evidence (color change, gas, odor, heat).
• Melting and freezing are physical changes; burning and rusting are chemical changes.

slides.title: Physical and Chemical Changes
slides.content:
Grade 4 — Quarter 1: Matter and Materials
(Validated Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

Learn to spot the crucial scientific difference: Has a new substance been formed?

slides.title: Physical Change: No New Material
slides.content:
The core rule of physical changes:
• The size, shape, or state/form of the material may change, but NO NEW MATERIAL IS FORMED.
• Cutting, folding, tearing, crushing
• Phase changes: Melting ice, freezing water, boiling soup
• Dissolving: Sugar dissolved in water can be recovered by evaporation!

slides.title: Chemical Change: New Substance Created
slides.content:
Evidence of chemical transformation:
• Burning: Wood turns into smoke, heat, and ash
• Rusting: Shiny steel turns into crumbly reddish-brown iron oxide
• Decaying: Organic matter breaks down into foul gases and humus
• The original substance cannot simply be folded or frozen back!
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Check original material
Step 2: Observe the process (heat, gas, color shift)
Step 3: Test: Is a brand new material formed?
Step 4: YES = Chemical Change; NO = Physical Change

slides.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
slides.content:
Quick Identification Guide:
• Cutting paper -> Physical (still paper fibers)
• Burning paper -> Chemical (produces ash and smoke)
• Melting chocolate -> Physical (cooling solidifies it again)
• Spoiled milk -> Chemical (acids create sour curd)

slides.title: Assessment: Physical vs Chemical
slides.content:
Check Your Understanding (Validated Answer Key: 1-B, 2-C, 3-D, 4-A, 5-B):
1. Folding paper into an airplane is a physical change (B)
2. Physical changes: size, shape, or state changes, but no new material is formed (C)
3. Wood burning into smoke and ash is clear evidence of chemical change (D)
4. Rusting iron is chemical because iron and oxygen form a new substance (A)
5. Dissolving sugar is physical because no new substance is formed (B)

customLessons.title: Responsible Use and Management of Materials
objectives: Identify ways to minimize harmful effects of improper use and management of materials in school and community.
Explain how science helps identify materials-related problems (pollution, clogged drainage) and suggest responsible actions.
Practice safe handling and storage of household materials (avoid burning waste, keep original containers, ask adults for help).
customLessons.content:
GRADE 4 SCIENCE — LESSON 5: Responsible Use and Management of Materials
(Validated DepEd MATATAG Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

LEARNING COMPETENCY:
1. Identify ways to minimize harmful effects of improper use and management of materials.
2. Identify materials-related issues in school/community and explain how science can help address them.

HARMFUL EFFECTS OF IMPROPER USE AND MANAGEMENT OF MATERIALS:
• Burning Household Waste: Releases toxic fumes, smoke particles, and greenhouse gases that trigger asthma and air pollution. Refinement rule: Avoid burning household waste and follow proper waste-management practices!
• Improper Waste Disposal: Dumping plastic wrappers into streets and canals causes clogged drainage systems and severe community flooding during monsoon rains.
• Unsafe Chemical Storage: Keeping pesticides or bleach in unlabeled beverage bottles risks accidental poisoning among young children.

SAFE PRACTICES FOR PUPILS:
1. Follow instructions on product labels carefully.
2. Never taste, smell, or handle unknown substances.
3. Keep cleaning products in original labeled containers.
4. Always ask an adult, parent, or teacher for assistance when using household chemicals.

HOW SCIENCE HELPS OUR COMMUNITY:
Science helps identify pollution problems, invents recyclable materials, and designs composting systems to convert organic waste into rich soil fertilizer.

INTERACTIVE ACTIVITY: Problem → Safe Action!
• Situation 1: Scattered plastic wrappers in the canal → Action: Segregate and place in recycling bins to prevent clogged drains.
• Situation 2: Smoldering pile of dried leaves → Action: Extinguish safely and transfer leaves to an organic compost pit.
• Situation 3: Bleach stored in an old soda bottle → Action: Ask an adult to transfer to a labeled safety bottle out of children's reach.
• Situation 4: Spent flashlight batteries → Action: Place in special hazardous e-waste collection bin.
• Situation 5: Leftover vegetable peels from cooking → Action: Mix with soil and brown leaves in the garden compost.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Avoid burning waste; practice the 5Rs (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Repair, Refuse).
• Proper waste disposal prevents clogged canals and street floods.
• Safe storage in original containers prevents chemical accidents.
• Science empowers us to make responsible decisions for our environment.

slides.title: Responsible Use and Management
slides.content:
Grade 4 — Quarter 1: Matter and Materials
(Validated Curriculum — Bay Central Elementary School)

Learn how safe handling, proper disposal, and environmental science protect homes and communities.

slides.title: Harmful Effects of Improper Disposal
slides.content:
Why improper management hurts us:
• Burning Waste: Releases toxic smoke that damages lungs and pollutes air
• Clogged Drainage: Plastic debris blocks canals, causing rapid flash flooding
• Safe action: Avoid burning household waste and follow proper waste-management practices!

slides.title: Core Safety Rules with Chemicals
slides.content:
Protecting yourself and family:
1. Keep all materials in original containers with clear warning labels
2. Never taste, inhale, or play with unknown substances
3. Store cleaners in high cabinets away from food
4. Always ask an adult or teacher for help!
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Check container label
Step 2: Never transfer chemicals into juice bottles
Step 3: Wear protective gear if instructed
Step 4: Ask an adult for guidance

slides.title: Science Solutions: The 5Rs & Composting
slides.content:
How science helps our community:
• Segregate Waste: Green bin (biodegradable) & Blue bin (recyclable)
• Composting: Turning food scraps into rich fertilizer instead of throwing them away
• 5Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Repair, Refuse single-use plastics!

slides.title: Assessment: Responsible Management
slides.content:
Check Your Understanding (Validated Answer Key: 1-A, 2-B, 3-B, 4-A, 5-C):
1. Burning plastic waste releases toxic smoke and dangerous pollutants into air (A)
2. Dumping plastics in gutters causes clogged drainage and community flooding (B)
3. Safest practice: Keep cleaners in original labeled containers and ask adults (B)
4. Science helps by identifying harmful waste effects and developing recycling (A)
5. Segregating waste into recycling bins demonstrates the 5Rs at school (C)
